# Emission–Absorption Composite Profile

## Motivation

Line-finding algorithms such as CWT frequently identify emission peaks and absorption troughs independently.

When an absorption feature is superposed on an emission line of the same species, the resulting profile may be fragmented into multiple detections:

* a central trough identified as an absorption line;
* one or more adjacent maxima identified as emission lines;
* additional local extrema generated by noise.

Treating these detections independently can lead to incorrect line assignments.

Whenever an emission line and an absorption line of the same transition are detected at nearly the same wavelength, they should be evaluated as a possible composite system.

---

## Physical Interpretation

A composite profile occurs when:

1. a broad or narrow emission line is present;
2. absorbing material along the line of sight removes flux near the line center;
3. the observed profile becomes an emission feature containing a central depression.

The absorption does not necessarily represent an independent spectral feature.

Instead, it may be modifying the shape of a single underlying emission line.

---

## Morphological Signature

A genuine emission–absorption composite profile typically exhibits:

* a central absorption trough;
* emission wings on both sides of the trough;
* smooth flux continuity between components;
* approximate symmetry around a common center.

Conceptually:

```text
Flux

 ^
 |
 |          /\        /\
 |         /  \______/  \
 |        /              \
 |_______/________________\____> λ
```

The profile resembles a broad "M" shape.

Interpretation:

```text
left wing   absorption   right wing
     \          |          /
      \         |         /
       \________|________/
            same line
```

The two apparent peaks are not necessarily separate emission lines.

They may be the two surviving shoulders of a single emission profile.

---

## Diagnostic Criteria

### Criterion 1: Common Central Wavelength

The absorption trough should lie near the center of the emission structure.

Expected:

```text
λ_abs ≈ λ_emission_center
```

For a split profile:

```text
λ_abs ≈ (λ_left + λ_right)/2
```

Large offsets weaken the interpretation.

---

### Criterion 2: Broad and Smooth Wings

Real composite systems generally preserve the morphology of the parent emission line.

The two wings should therefore appear:

* broad,
* smooth,
* continuous.

Example:

```text
      /\        /\
     /  \______/  \
    /              \
```

Preferred over:

```text
      /\    /\
       \____/
```

where both peaks are narrow spikes.

---

### Criterion 3: Approximate Symmetry

The left and right sides should have comparable:

* width,
* curvature,
* extent,
* amplitude.

Perfect symmetry is not required.

However, severe asymmetry often indicates either:

* noise contamination,
* incorrect line identification,
* blending with another transition.

---

### Criterion 4: Continuum Connectivity

The wings should merge naturally into the surrounding continuum.

Profiles composed of isolated spikes with no broad structure are less reliable.

---

## Warning Signs

### Noise-Induced False Composite

```text
      /\_/\/\__/\/\_
```

Multiple local extrema without a coherent broad profile.

Interpretation:

* emission detection likely spurious;
* absorption detection likely spurious.

---

### Spike–Valley–Spike Pattern

```text
      /\    /\
       \____/
```

Two narrow peaks surrounding a trough.

Interpretation:

* commonly produced by noise fluctuations;
* does not strongly support a physical composite system.

---

### Strongly Asymmetric Structure

```text
           /\
          /  \____
      /\_/
```

Only one side exhibits a broad emission wing.

Interpretation:

* may indicate line blending,
* may indicate an incorrect absorption assignment,
* should not automatically be interpreted as a composite profile.

---

## Recommended Agent Behavior

When an emission line and an absorption line of the same species are detected:

1. Search for a shared morphological structure.
2. Estimate the center of the combined profile.
3. Evaluate:

   * center consistency,
   * wing broadness,
   * smoothness,
   * symmetry.
4. If a coherent composite profile is present:

   * treat the detections as a single physical system;
   * increase confidence in the line identification.
5. If the profile is dominated by spikes or noise:

   * reduce confidence for both detections.

---

## Examples

### Mg II + Mg II_abs

A broad Mg II emission line split by a central absorption trough.

Common in quasars and BAL-related systems.

Typical morphology:

```text
        /\      /\
       /  \____/  \
```

---

### Hα + Hα_abs

Broad or narrow Hα emission with stellar or interstellar absorption near the center.

Often observed in galaxy spectra containing mixed stellar and nebular components.

---

### Hβ + Hβ_abs

A common case in post-starburst galaxies and stellar-dominated systems.

The underlying Balmer absorption may partially remove the nebular emission core, producing a composite profile.

---

## General Principle

A line should not be classified solely from individual local extrema.

Whenever an emission feature and an absorption feature of the same transition coexist at nearly identical wavelengths, the morphology of the entire profile should take precedence over the individual detections.
